1 # Package sync — user requirements 2 3 What package synchronisation is for, how it decides what to do, and what it asks you. Written to be read end to end: someone who finishes it should be able to predict what the tool does in a situation this document never mentions. 4 5 ## Navigation 6 7 - [High level requirements](high-level-requirements.md) — project vision and scope; this document elaborates "installed packages must sync" 8 - [Package sync conformance criteria](package-sync-conformance-criteria.md) — the same requirements of this document, decomposed into individually checkable obligations, for reviewing an implementation against 9 - [Package sync job behaviour](../jobs/package-sync.md) — user guide 10 - [ADR-020](../adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md) — the decision record behind the model 11 12 This document states the intent. Where it and any other document disagree, this one is right and the other needs fixing. 13 14 ## What package sync is for 15 16 You work on one machine, sync, and resume on the other. That only works if the software is there. Syncing your home directory onto a machine that lacks the applications gives you configuration files for programs that will not start, dotfiles for shells you do not have, and project directories you cannot build. 17 18 So package sync replicates *what software is installed*. It does not replicate application data — that is the folder sync's job. Folder sync must run after package sync: installing software writes that software's own stock defaults, and those defaults must land before your synced settings go on top of them. Get that order wrong and every package synced silently overwrites your configuration with the vendor's. 19 20 It replicates by **convergence, not by copying**. Nothing reads or writes another machine's package database or installed software. What travels between the machines is a decision — "install this", "remove that" — plus the minimum configuration the target's own `apt`, `snap` or `flatpak` package managers needs in order to carry it out. The target's package managers stay in charge of their own state, which is what keeps the target a working machine rather than one carrying another machine's bookkeeping. 21 22 You opt in per ecosystem. Nothing here runs unless you enable it, because enabling it authorises pc-switcher to install and remove software on the other machine. You can sync apt packages and not snaps, or flatpaks and nothing else. The four kinds of software are described in their own sections below and each is independently enableable, independently reviewed, and independently able to fail without taking the others down. 23 24 Which internal component owns which kind of software is an implementation detail and is expected to change. Nothing in this document depends on it. 25 26 ## Vocabulary 27 28 These words are used precisely throughout. Most of the ambiguity in earlier drafts came from not having them. 29 30 **Source** and **target** are per-run roles, not machines. You launch the sync on the source; the target is the machine being changed. The next run may swap them. 31 32 **The holding machine** is the machine that *has* the thing being decided about. For something the source has and the target lacks, the source holds it. For something only the target has, the target holds it. This is not the same as "the machine you are sitting at" — you are always at the source, but the holding machine is frequently the target. It matters because permanent decisions are stored on the holding machine. 33 34 An **item** is one thing you can be asked about: a package, a snap, a flatpak application, an apt hold, a mask, a configuration file. Every item has a stable identity that survives across runs, which is what lets a decision about it be remembered. 35 36 A **diff** is one item's difference between the two machines, together with what would be done about it — install, remove, change, or merely report. 37 38 A **decision** is your answer to a diff: apply it, skip it this once, or never offer it again on the holding machine. 39 40 **Derived mechanism** is plumbing that travels because something you approved needs it, and is therefore never a question of its own: the repository a package comes from, the signing key that makes that repository trusted, the pin that makes a vendor's build win, the remote a flatpak application installs from. 41 42 An **origin** (or **vendor**) is where a piece of software actually comes from — a repository URL, a flatpak remote's URL. Not its name: two remotes can share a name and serve different vendors. 43 44 **Machine-specific** describes an item you have marked as never to be offered again on the holding machine. 45 46 A **snippet** is a shell recipe you write once for software no package manager can install, stored and replayed verbatim. 47 48 **Scope** (flatpak only) is the user or system installation. **Revision** and **channel** (snap only) are the exact build and the update track. 49 50 ## The model 51 52 Five ideas. Everything else in this document follows from them, and most of the tool's behaviour is predictable from them alone. 53 54 **The source states intent; the target's own managers do the work.** The source machine's installed state is the only statement of what should exist. The target answers read-only questions while the change is planned, then carries out what you approved. A sync never modifies the source's software. 55 56 **Identity includes provenance where an ecosystem has more than one vendor.** `gh` from GitHub's repository and `gh` from Ubuntu's archive share a name and are different software. So for apt and flatpak a package is identified by name *and* origin, and the tool will not satisfy an approved install from a vendor the source does not use. Snap needs none of this: there is one store, and a name resolves to one publisher through an assertion snapd validates itself, so there is no second `firefox` to install by mistake. 57 58 **You are asked about software; the plumbing is derived.** Approving a package answers the question of whether its repository should exist — a repository approved without its package does nothing, and a package approved without its repository cannot be installed, so the pair was never separately expressible. The test is derivability: if the answer follows from something you already approved, you are not asked again. Where it does not follow, you are asked. There are exactly four such questions, and each is described where it arises. 59 60 **Consent precedes every change.** Nothing is written to the target before you have approved that ecosystem's diff. Questions are gathered into one review per ecosystem wherever possible — a question per package is the interruption the review exists to replace — but that is a strong preference, not a prohibition. An approved action can establish facts that were unknowable before it landed, and asking a further question then is correct. What this permits is a second question, not a queue of them. Approving a removal always takes a gesture distinct from approving an install, and is never the default. 61 62 **A failure belongs to the smallest thing it can.** Every approved item is attempted; a failure is collected against that item, named, and the run continues. One failed item does not stop its ecosystem, and one failed ecosystem does not stop the others. 63 64 ```mermaid 65 flowchart LR 66 A["plan
(reads only)"] --> B["review
(your decisions)"] 67 B --> C["apply
(one item at a time)"] 68 C --> D["report
(per item)"] 69 A -.->|"nothing is written
before the review returns"| C 70 ``` 71 72 ## One run, start to finish 73 74 Everything enabled, both machines healthy. This is the shape of a sync; the ecosystem sections that follow add detail without changing it. 75 76 **Before anything runs**, each enabled ecosystem checks its own preconditions and the run refuses to start if any fail, with copy-paste remedies. The requirements differ and are worth knowing, because they are the most common reason a first sync will not start: 77 78 | Ecosystem | Passwordless sudo on the source | Passwordless sudo on the target | 79 | - | - | - | 80 | apt | required | required | 81 | snap | required | required | 82 | flatpak | not needed | only when a system-scope item exists on either machine | 83 | unreproducible software | not needed | not needed | 84 85 apt needs it on the source because reading `/etc/apt` needs root — and without it the read silently returns nothing, which would report a successful sync that replicated no repository configuration at all. snap needs it on both because the run pauses auto-refresh on both machines, and because snapd requires admin rights even to *read* its configuration. flatpak asks for nothing it will not use. Snippets need nothing, because whatever privilege a snippet wants is written inside the snippet. 86 87 apt additionally refuses to start while the target's dpkg lock is held — usually unattended-upgrades — because there is no useful way to proceed. 88 89 **The run then pauses snap auto-refresh on both machines.** snapd refreshes several times a day and would otherwise move a revision out from under the sync. The pause is timed, so it expires on its own if the run crashes, and each machine's previous setting is captured and restored afterwards — including an indefinite hold you set yourself. If a machine's previous setting cannot be read, that machine's policy is left alone rather than cleared. 90 91 **Each ecosystem then runs in turn**, and each does the same four things. 92 93 It **plans**, issuing read commands only. It asks both machines what they have, applies your standing decisions, and works out the differences. For apt this starts by reading `/etc/apt` on both machines, because a package's classification depends on which repository file declares its origin. 94 95 It **asks** anything that cannot be derived. apt's Ubuntu Pro question is asked here, before any other planning, because one of its answers ends the job and there is no sense making you answer a review you would then throw away. 96 97 It **reviews**. You get one screen per group of same-kind, same-direction items — one screen of installs, a separate screen of removals, and so on. Every item is a row, and every row carries its own decision in a column beside it. Arrows move between rows, one key sets the focused row's answer, and Enter confirms the screen. Nothing is echoed back afterwards: the answered list stays on screen, and that is the record. 98 99 Rows start where confirming the screen unread would do no harm — installs start at *apply*, and anything that removes, deletes, or overwrites something the machine already has starts at *skip*. Three answers are offered where a permanent decision is meaningful and two where it is not, and the difference you see is a shorter legend rather than a different kind of screen. 100 101 Every screen names your machines. It says `p17` and `fleksi`, never "the source" and "the target" — those are roles this run happens to assign, and making you work out which of your two computers a line means before you can answer it defeats the question. For the same reason each answer states its own effect on a named machine rather than the mechanism behind it: on a removal screen the skip answer reads *keep it on fleksi*, and on a conflict screen *keep fleksi's version*, because that is the half of the decision you are actually weighing. 102 103 Ctrl-C at any screen aborts the whole sync. It is never read as declining one item. 104 105 It **applies**, one item at a time, in an order the ecosystem requires — for apt, the repository configuration lands before the packages that need it, and holds land last, after the packages they name exist. Every write is announced. Nothing that was not approved is written. 106 107 **When everything has run**, the snap refresh policy is restored and each ecosystem reports: success if it did what you approved (including doing nothing because the machines already matched), skipped if it deliberately did nothing and said why, failed if at least one approved item could not be applied — with each failure naming its item. 108 109 You can rehearse all of this with a dry run. The rehearsal plans and reviews exactly as a real run does, including asking you the questions, and then issues no command that changes either machine. It also previews the derived writes, which have no review line of their own — a rehearsal that showed an `apt-get update` and no reason for it would be worse than useless. Nothing is recorded, no snippet is written, no registry is transferred. 110 111 You can also run with `--confirm-each-command`, which shows every individual modification verbatim and applies it only after you say so. It offers proceed or abort and no third answer, because one reviewed item spans several commands and skipping one would leave the item half-applied. It covers every write, including the files that record your own decisions. 112 113 A run with no terminal asks nothing. Every reviewable item is treated as declined for that run, nothing is recorded, and any ecosystem with a non-empty review reports skipped rather than claiming success for work it did not do. 114 115 ## Decisions and their memory 116 117 Three answers, and where the third one lives. 118 119 **Apply** does the thing. **Skip** declines it for this run and records nothing, so it is offered again next sync. **Always skip** marks the item machine-specific, and that is where the interesting question is: *which* machine. 120 121 All three are answers to one question on one screen, not a first pass and a second pass over the leftovers. That matters because "apply" and "never offer this again" are opposite answers to the same question, and splitting them across two screens made them look like answers to two different ones. 122 123 The mark is stored on the **holding machine** — the machine that has the item. Not the machine you launched from, and not the machine you answered on. 124 125 Worked example. You are on P17. XPS13 has `steam` installed; P17 does not. The sync offers to remove `steam` from XPS13. You answer "never offer again". The mark is written **on XPS13**, because XPS13 is the machine that holds `steam`. You made the decision on P17, sitting at P17, about software that only exists on XPS13 — and the record of it lands on XPS13. The next sync, in either direction, finds it there and says nothing about `steam` at all. 126 127 The other direction works the same way. P17 has `wireshark`; XPS13 does not. The sync offers to install it on XPS13. You answer "never offer again", and the mark is written on **P17**, the holding machine, because the thing being decided about is P17's copy. 128 129 Once marked, an item is inert on that machine in both roles: never pushed out when it is the source, never installed or removed when it is the target. It is filtered out before any difference is computed, so it produces no review line in any later run — it becomes structurally invisible. That invisibility is deliberate and it has a cost, which shows up twice below: because a machine-specific package never appears in a review, something else has to tell you when a change would strand it or move where it comes from. Those are the repository-deletion and repository-conflict disclosures. 130 131 Marks never travel between machines. A new machine means deciding again — which is the point, since the whole meaning of the mark is "this machine is different". 132 133 Snippets go the other way and **do** travel, because how to install something is knowledge about the software, not about the machine. 134 135 Two things you cannot mark, and the reason is the same for both. Deleting a repository, deleting a pin, resolving a repository conflict, and deleting or repointing a flatpak remote all take two answers — do it, or leave it for now — and record nothing. A permanent machine-local mark on configuration whose whole purpose is to feed software would silently and permanently change where that software comes from. Where two machines' configurations genuinely differ on purpose, the remedy is to consolidate them, not to record a preference that quietly diverges them further.

The requirements differ and are worth knowing, because they are the most common reason a first sync will not start: | Ecosystem | Passwordless sudo on the source | Passwordless sudo on the target | | - | - | - | | apt | required | required | | snap | required | required | | flatpak | not needed | only when a system-scope item exists on either machine | | unreproducible software | not needed | not needed | apt needs it on the source because reading `/etc/apt` needs root — and without it the read silently returns nothing, which would report a successful sync that replicated no repository configuration at all. snap needs it on both because the run pauses auto-refresh on both machines, and because snapd requires admin rights even to *read* its configuration. flatpak asks for nothing it will not use. Snippets need nothing, because whatever privilege a snippet wants is written inside the snippet. apt additionally refuses to start while the target's dpkg lock is held — usually unattended-upgrades — because there is no useful way to proceed. **The run then pauses snap auto-refresh on both machines.** snapd refreshes several times a day and would otherwise move a revision out from under the sync. The pause is timed, so it expires on its own if the run crashes, and each machine's previous setting is captured and restored afterwards — including an indefinite hold you set yourself. If a machine's previous setting cannot be read, that machine's policy is left alone rather than cleared. **Each ecosystem then runs in turn**, and each does the same four things. It **plans**, issuing read commands only. It asks both machines what they have, applies your standing decisions, and works out the differences. For apt this starts by reading `/etc/apt` on both machines, because a package's classification depends on which repository file declares its origin. It **asks** anything that cannot be derived. apt's Ubuntu Pro question is asked here, before any other planning, because one of its answers ends the job and there is no sense making you answer a review you would then throw away. It **reviews**. You get one screen per group of same-kind, same-direction items — one screen of installs, a separate screen of removals, and so on. Every item is a row, and every row carries its own decision in a column beside it. Arrows move between rows, one key sets the focused row's answer, and Enter confirms the screen. Nothing is echoed back afterwards: the answered list stays on screen, and that is the record. Rows start where confirming the screen unread would do no harm — installs start at *apply*, and anything that removes, deletes, or overwrites something the machine already has starts at *skip*. Three answers are offered where a permanent decision is meaningful and two where it is not, and the difference you see is a shorter legend rather than a different kind of screen. Every screen names your machines. It says `p17` and `fleksi`, never "the source" and "the target" — those are roles this run happens to assign, and making you work out which of your two computers a line means before you can answer it defeats the question. For the same reason each answer states its own effect on a named machine rather than the mechanism behind it: on a removal screen the skip answer reads *keep it on fleksi*, and on a conflict screen *keep fleksi's version*, because that is the half of the decision you are actually weighing. Ctrl-C at any screen aborts the whole sync. It is never read as declining one item. It **applies**, one item at a time, in an order the ecosystem requires — for apt, the repository configuration lands before the packages that need it, and holds land last, after the packages they name exist. Every write is announced. Nothing that was not approved is written. **When everything has run**, the snap refresh policy is restored and each ecosystem reports: success if it did what you approved (including doing nothing because the machines already matched), skipped if it deliberately did nothing and said why, failed if at least one approved item could not be applied — with each failure naming its item. You can rehearse all of this with a dry run. The rehearsal plans and reviews exactly as a real run does, including asking you the questions, and then issues no command that changes either machine. It also previews the derived writes, which have no review line of their own — a rehearsal that showed an `apt-get update` and no reason for it would be worse than useless. Nothing is recorded, no snippet is written, no registry is transferred. You can also run with `--confirm-each-command`, which shows every individual modification verbatim and applies it only after you say so. It offers proceed or abort and no third answer, because one reviewed item spans several commands and skipping one would leave the item half-applied. It covers every write, including the files that record your own decisions. A run with no terminal asks nothing. Every reviewable item is treated as declined for that run, nothing is recorded, and any ecosystem with a non-empty review reports skipped rather than claiming success for work it did not do. ## Decisions and their memory Three answers, and where the third one lives. **Apply** does the thing. **Skip** declines it for this run and records nothing, so it is offered again next sync. **Always skip** marks the item machine-specific, and that is where the interesting question is: *which* machine. All three are answers to one question on one screen, not a first pass and a second pass over the leftovers. That matters because "apply" and "never offer this again" are opposite answers to the same question, and splitting them across two screens made them look like answers to two different ones. The mark is stored on the **holding machine** — the machine that has the item. Not the machine you launched from, and not the machine you answered on. Worked example. You are on P17. XPS13 has `steam` installed; P17 does not. The sync offers to remove `steam` from XPS13. You answer "never offer again". The mark is written **on XPS13**, because XPS13 is the machine that holds `steam`. You made the decision on P17, sitting at P17, about software that only exists on XPS13 — and the record of it lands on XPS13. The next sync, in either direction, finds it there and says nothing about `steam` at all. The other direction works the same way. P17 has `wireshark`; XPS13 does not. The sync offers to install it on XPS13. You answer "never offer again", and the mark is written on **P17**, the holding machine, because the thing being decided about is P17's copy. Once marked, an item is inert on that machine in both roles: never pushed out when it is the source, never installed or removed when it is the target. It is filtered out before any difference is computed, so it produces no review line in any later run — it becomes structurally invisible. That invisibility is deliberate and it has a cost, which shows up twice below: because a machine-specific package never appears in a review, something else has to tell you when a change would strand it or move where it comes from. Those are the repository-deletion and repository-conflict disclosures. Marks never travel between machines. A new machine means deciding again — which is the point, since the whole meaning of the mark is "this machine is different". Snippets go the other way and **do** travel, because how to install something is knowledge about the software, not about the machine. Two things you cannot mark, and the reason is the same for both. Deleting a repository, deleting a pin, resolving a repository conflict, and deleting or repointing a flatpak remote all take two answers — do it, or leave it for now — and record nothing. A permanent machine-local mark on configuration whose whole purpose is to feed software would silently and permanently change where that software comes from. Where two machines' configurations genuinely differ on purpose, the remedy is to consolidate them, not to record a preference that quietly diverges them further.

135 Two things you cannot mark, and the reason is the same for both. Deleting a repository, deleting a pin, resolving a repository conflict, and deleting or repointing a flatpak remote all take two answers — do it, or leave it for now — and record nothing. A permanent machine-local mark on configuration whose whole purpose is to feed software would silently and permanently change where that software comes from. Where two machines' configurations genuinely differ on purpose, the remedy is to consolidate them, not to record a preference that quietly diverges them further. 136 137 Report-only findings — a version difference, a cross-vendor divergence, a package whose origin cannot be replicated — cannot be marked either. No machine holds a version difference. A permanent mark there would stop the package syncing altogether rather than stop reporting the drift, which is not what you would be asking for. These are resolved by fixing the underlying condition. 138 139 ## apt 140 141 apt carries every hard problem, so it gets the most space. The other ecosystems are largely apt with pieces removed. 142 143 Scope is the **manually installed** package set — what you asked for, not what apt pulled in to satisfy it. Dependencies are the target apt's business to resolve for itself. Along with the packages come the repositories and pins that govern where they come from, apt's own behavioural configuration, and apt holds. 144 145 ### Installing 146 147 A package the source has and the target lacks is offered for install. What it takes to make that install faithful depends on where the source got it. 148 149 ```mermaid 150 flowchart TD 151 A["On the source,
absent on the target"] --> B{"Where did the
source get it?"} 152 B -->|"the distribution"| C["Ordinary install"] 153 B -->|"a vendor"| D{"Does the target already
offer it from that vendor?"} 154 D -->|yes| C 155 D -->|no| E{"Can the source's origin
be replicated?"} 156 E -->|yes| F["Install, naming the vendor.
Its repository, key and pin
travel as a consequence"] 157 E -->|no| G["Report it, with origin
and reason. Do not install"] 158 F --> H{"After the configuration lands,
what would apt really install?"} 159 H -->|"the source's vendor"| I["Install"] 160 H -->|otherwise| J["Refuse this one install,
naming both origins.
Continue the run"] 161 ``` 162 163 Two things about that diagram carry most of the weight. 164 165 When an install would come from anything other than the distribution, the review says which vendor — you should not approve `gh` without knowing it is arriving from GitHub rather than from Ubuntu. 166 167 And the last step is a real check, not a formality. Everything before it is preparation; only that step looks at what the target's apt would *actually* do after this run's configuration has landed and its package lists have been refreshed. A repository can fail to write, a pin can fail to win, and Ubuntu's own epoch can outrank every version a vendor publishes. So the guarantee is verified against the target's real state rather than inferred from the plan, and an install that would come from the wrong place fails as its own item naming both origins, while everything else in the run proceeds. 168 169 Two machines pointed at different Ubuntu mirrors are not two vendors. Each machine's own distribution source files define what "the distribution" means for that machine, so mirror differences never read as provenance differences. 170 171 Software installed from a hand-downloaded `.deb` is not apt's business at all — apt on the target has never heard the name, so an apt item for it could only fail. It belongs to the unreproducible-software section below. 172 173 ### Removing, and reporting without acting 174 175 A package on the target that the source does not have is offered for removal, in its own unticked group. Approving it removes the package without purging its configuration. 176 177 A package present on both machines at the same version from the same vendor produces nothing at all — no line, no question. 178 179 Three situations are reported and never acted on. 180 181 Same package, same vendor, different version: both versions are named and nothing is done. Versions float — you install by name and take whatever the target's repositories offer. Deliberate pinning still replicates, through the pin files, which is the honest way to hold a version. 182 183 Same package, two different vendors: reported as a provenance divergence naming both origins, and it takes precedence over any version difference on that package, because two vendors' builds share no version scale. Converging it would mean a cross-vendor reinstall you never asked for, and neither machine is wrong — only you can say which one is the odd one out. 184 185 A package whose origin cannot be replicated at all — no repository file on the source declares it, or the one that does names a key the source does not have — is reported with the origin and the reason, and never installed from somewhere else. 186 187 A package held on the target is never proposed for install or upgrade and produces no package-level line. Its hold is still an item of its own. 188 189 ### Holds 190 191 An apt hold replicates as its own item, decided separately from the package it applies to, in both directions. You may want a package synced and its hold not, or the reverse. 192 193 An approved hold is applied after the package it names exists. Replicating a hold never changes the package's version, and a hold whose package failed to install fails alone. 194 195 ### Collateral damage 196 197 Approving an install can make apt remove something else. Whether you are asked depends on what that something else is. 198 199 If it was installed automatically — apt pulled it in to satisfy some other package — the removal proceeds silently. That is the target's apt resolving its own dependency graph, and it is not a decision you have information to make. 200 201 If it was **manually installed on the target**, you chose to have it, and you are asked before anything happens. The question names the package, says why it is protected — that machine's own apt has it marked manually installed, which is not the same as anyone having marked it machine-specific — and says what the approved change would do to it. Three answers, each stating its own effect: install anyway and accept the loss, skip and leave the triggering install unapproved, or stop. The stop answer says how far it reaches, because it ends the whole sync rather than this one ecosystem. 202 203 The question is asked during the review, from apt's own simulation of the transaction, not as an interruption while packages are being installed. 204 205 Declining cancels only the changes whose own transaction causes the collateral. This matters more than it sounds: the other answers in that review are yours, given about other software, and a decline that reached them would be a decision you did not make. So when a batch turns up manual collateral, each candidate is rehearsed on its own to find out which ones are actually responsible. Where the collateral is caused by a combination and by no single change, the whole set is cancelled and the question says so. 206 207 Cancelling a change this way never alters a decision you gave for it. A package you marked "never offer again" keeps that mark even though the collateral cancelled it for this run. 208 209 There is one case where you are told afterwards rather than asked beforehand: an install whose repository this very run must provision. Until that repository lands, the target's apt cannot resolve the name, and asking apt to rehearse a batch containing an unknown name makes it refuse the entire batch — which would strip the protection from every other package in the run rather than weaken it for one. Those packages are rehearsed individually after the repository configuration has converged, and unapproved manual collateral fails that one install. 210 211 ### Repositories, keys and pins 212 213 You are never asked to add or change a repository. A repository is written to the target because a package you approved comes from it, and a repository on the source that feeds no package this run syncs does not travel at all. 214 215 Deleting one is different, because nothing derives a deletion. A repository the target has and the source does not is offered for removal with two answers. The request names the repository URLs the file declares, not just its filename — a filename is whatever created the file chose to call it, and the URL is what the deletion actually takes away — and it names the machine-specific packages on that machine that the deletion would strand. That second disclosure exists precisely because those packages are invisible in the review by design; without it you would see a bare file deletion and nothing else. It is disclosure, not refusal: deleting a repository whose packages are going too is ordinary cleanup. 216 217 A repository present on both machines with different content is normally overwritten with the source's version, silently — you asked for the two machines to match. There is one exception. If that file feeds a package the target marked machine-specific, overwriting it would move the origin of software you explicitly told this tool to leave alone, and nothing else in the run would mention it. So you are asked first, shown **both versions of the file in full** — target's first, source's second, never a computed diff, because a diff of two repository definitions is not readable — and given two answers. Nothing is recorded either way. Declining is not a no-op: every approved package whose origin depended on that file fails by name, rather than being installed from somewhere else. 218 219 The distribution's own source files are written when the target lacks them, overwritten when they differ, and never removed or offered for removal. They are what defines "the distribution's own origin" on each machine, which is what stops two machines on different mirrors disagreeing about every package. 220 221 Files apt itself does not read — the `.save` and `.orig` copies Ubuntu's tooling leaves behind — are not treated as repository configuration in any direction. 222 223 **Signing keys are never a review item, in any direction.** You think in repositories and packages; a key is only how a repository is made to work. A key the target lacks is copied byte-for-byte from the source before the repository naming it is written, whatever owns it on the source — vendors ship `.deb` packages carrying both a repository entry and its key, so refusing to copy a package-owned key would make such a repository permanently untrustable. A key the target has with different bytes is refreshed, which is what makes a vendor's key rotation follow you even though rotation changes no repository file; the exception is a key the target's own distribution packaging owns, which is left alone. A key that already matches is untouched. Keys are never fetched from a vendor. 224 225 When you approve deleting a repository, a key that nothing on the target references any more may be deleted with it. That count is taken against the target's real files after the run's writes, so a repository you left unticked, one marked machine-specific, and one this tool never syncs all keep their keys alive. Only the directory that exists purely for this purpose is ever cleaned up; ambient and distribution-owned trust is left to accumulate rather than deleted on a guess. 226 227 Pins are the one exception to derivation. **Every** pin file the source has is written to the target, always, without review. A pin decides which origin wins, which is exactly what origin replication turns on, and a pin naming an origin the target does not have does nothing at all — so replicating them all costs nothing and cannot get a per-package derivation wrong. The price is that a pin you wanted on one machine only comes back every run; deleting it on the source is the only cure. Deleting a pin the target has and the source does not *is* reviewed, because removing it can flip which vendor supplies a package at that machine's next upgrade. The screen prints each offered pin file whole, one block per file, for the same reason the repository deletion names URLs: a name like `99-vendor.pref` tells you neither which origin it favours nor at what priority, and those are the whole content of the decision. 228 229 A pin is never read as a statement about the packages it names. A machine-wide pin would otherwise report every package on the machine, and would make a target-only package impossible to remove and impossible to silence. 230 231 apt's own behavioural configuration — proxy settings, recommends policy, the things that govern how apt behaves rather than where packages come from — is reviewed in all three directions with the full decision including the permanent mark. No approved package implies whether such a setting should travel, and it is exactly the kind of standing preference you genuinely hold per machine. 232 233 ### Ubuntu Pro 234 235 If the source carries ESM repositories and the target reports no Ubuntu Pro attachment, you are asked before anything is written and before any other apt question, with two answers: attach the target now, or skip apt entirely for this run while everything else proceeds. The screen tells you what to run on the target to attach it. 236 237 This is asked rather than handled because it cannot be handled: attaching needs a subscription token or an interactive browser flow, the source's own credentials are root-only and not reusable, and carrying a token would put a secret on a command line. 238 239 It is asked rather than ignored because ignoring it fails in a way you would never trace back to a sync. The ESM repository indexes are public, so an unattached target's `apt-get update` succeeds and the ESM versions win candidate selection — and the failure surfaces much later, as a 401 when apt fetches the actual package for some unrelated install. 240 241 Answering "I have attached it" re-probes the target rather than believing you, and you may answer as many times as you like. Skipping skips the whole apt job rather than only the ESM files, because pins always travel, so the source's ESM pins would otherwise land on a target without the sources they name — leaving a candidate selection that matches neither machine. An untouched configuration is a state you can reason about. 242 243 A run with nobody to ask takes the skip and says why. A dry run does not ask; it warns that a real run would skip apt, because a rehearsal must not send you off to attach a machine. 244 245 Only whether the target is attached is ever logged or shown. The attachment check also learns the subscriber's identity, and that never leaves it. 246 247 ### Applying apt's changes 248 249 All of the repository-configuration work a run does is applied as one unit: everything is backed up first, written in apt's own required order, and followed by a single refresh of the package lists. If that refresh fails, every file the unit touched is restored and `/etc/apt` is left exactly as it was found — a half-written configuration nobody reviewed is worse than either end state. Every approved package whose origin depended on that unit then fails, by name, and the run continues with the packages that did not. 250 251 If a restore itself fails, the backup is kept and its path is named, because it holds the only remaining copy of that file. 252 253 A derived write has no item of its own, so it cannot fail as one. Its failure is charged to every approved package that needed it, naming what failed — you decided about a package, not about a file. Every derived write is logged as it lands and appears in a dry run's preview: not asking is not the same as hiding. 254 255 ## snap 256 257 snap is the simple ecosystem with one sharp exception. 258 259 There is one store, and a name resolves to one publisher through an assertion snapd validates itself. So there is no origin question, no repository, no key, and no screen for any of them. Nothing about snap provenance is ever put to you. 260 261 The exception is that snap converges the source's **exact revision and tracking channel**, where apt and flatpak let versions float. The reason is that snap is the only ecosystem that puts the version number in the data path: per-user application data lives in `~/snap///`. If the two machines are on different revisions, folder sync has no correct thing to do — it would either skip the data or plant directories for revisions the target's snapd never installed. Converging the revision is what makes folder sync correct. 262 263 A snap on the source only is offered for install at the source's revision and channel; one on the target only is offered for removal; a difference of revision or channel is offered as a single change naming both values; identical produces nothing. Confinement travels with the install, because snapd requires it as explicit confirmation before it will install a classic or devmode revision at all. 264 265 Removing a snap leaves snapd's own pre-removal snapshot in place. That snapshot is your only recovery path if the removal was a mistake. 266 267 A snap whose revision the target cannot fetch fails as its own item and the run continues. 268 269 Refresh holds replicate as their own items in both directions, decided separately from the snap. A hold recorded for a snap the source no longer has produces no item — the source is authoritative for what you currently intend. No command this tool issues ever sets a standing hold as a side effect. 270 271 Sideloaded snaps — installed from a local `.snap` file rather than the store — cannot be reproduced by any snap command, because no store can serve their revision. Today they are named in a warning and dropped: no install is offered, and the target's matching entry is withheld too, so "cannot reproduce this" does not turn into "propose deleting it there". A sideloaded snap the source does *not* have is still an ordinary removal candidate. **This is a current gap rather than a settled outcome** — a snippet could reproduce one, and the intended fix is to hand them to the unreproducible-software path. See the open questions. 272 273 ## flatpak 274 275 flatpak repeats apt's origin problem with different mechanics and one structural difference: there is no distribution remote. A fresh flatpak installation has zero remotes configured, and a machine with none is perfectly ordinary. So there is no equivalent of apt's never-removed distribution sources — even Flathub travels only because something needs it. 276 277 An application is identified by its **scope** and its **full reference including branch**. The same application in the user and system installations is two independent items; so are two branches of one application. That is not a normalisation failure, it is what branches and scopes are for: two branches coexist side by side, and the two installations are configured separately. A scope or branch difference therefore reads as one install and one removal, and the tool reports it exactly as found. 278 279 Origin is deliberately *not* part of identity, because flatpak leaves no way to converge it: installing a ref you already have from a different remote is simply refused. So a cross-vendor difference is reported rather than acted on, and it takes precedence over a version difference on the same application. 280 281 Remotes are derived from the applications approved from them, and declining the application is the only way to decline the remote. Derivation covers the runtime too: an approved application pulls the runtime it is built against, and that runtime may come from a remote no directly-approved application uses. Every derived remote is provisioned before the first application installs. 282 283 **A remote replicates with its trust, not just its name and URL.** Whether the source verifies the remote's signatures travels, and where it does, its signing key travels too — copied byte-for-byte from the source, never fetched from a vendor. Without the key a replicated remote is configured but unusable, and every install from it fails. A remote the source verifies is never replicated as unverified. A remote the source itself does not verify is replicated unverified, and you are told. 284 285 A remote present on both machines whose URL or verification setting differs is repointed in place, silently, without disturbing the applications that name it — with the same exception apt has for repository files. If the repoint would move the origin of an application the target marked machine-specific, you are asked first, shown both configurations, told which applications are the reason, and given two answers with nothing recorded. The question is only raised about a remote this run would touch anyway — one no approved application needs is not repointed and so is not a question — which is narrower than apt's equivalent, where every differing repository file feeding machine-specific software is put to you and approving forces the write. Declining fails every approved application that needed the source's URL, citing your decision. A difference of key alone never raises the question, because importing a key merges into the remote's existing trust rather than replacing it — it can neither move an origin nor withdraw trust. 286 287 A remote present only on the target is offered for deletion, and the request names the applications on the target that still have it as their origin in that scope. Deleting a remote takes its signing key with it. 288 289 An application is installed from the source's remote or not at all, and that remote is identified by **URL and verification setting, never by name**. Two remotes can share a name and serve different vendors' builds, with success reported either way, and re-adding an existing remote name succeeds without changing where it points — so neither a matching name nor a successful add is evidence of anything. The check is therefore made against the target's own state before the install, and the landed origin is read back and resolved to a URL again afterwards. Either failure fails that one application, naming both URLs. 290 291 An application whose origin remote exists neither on the target nor among this run's own additions is refused as its own item naming the missing remote. 292 293 A remote the source restricts with a filter is replicated **unfiltered**, and the run warns once per such remote and tells you how to re-apply the filter on the target. A filter's content lives in an arbitrary local file outside flatpak's own store, and flatpak validates neither its path nor its existence — so it is not repository-or-key material that can travel, and a silent successful add would read as full replication when it is not. 294 295 Mask patterns replicate per scope, in both directions, whether or not anything currently matches them. A mask is a pure pattern, so editing one reads as remove-old plus add-new and a scope split reads as add plus remove — reported as found, not normalised. Masks land after the applications, so a mask can never suppress a dependency an approved install needs to pull in. 296 297 An installation that is neither the user nor the system one is skipped rather than guessed at. 298 299 A run touching only the user scope needs no root on the target. 300 301 ## Software no manager can reproduce 302 303 Everything above assumes a package manager on the target can be told to install the thing. This section is the complement: software that arrived on the source by some route nothing can replay automatically. 304 305 It is not one kind of thing. There are four, with genuinely different detection, and what they share is the **install snippet** — a shell recipe you write once, which then travels with the software rather than staying on the machine. 306 307 **A hand-downloaded `.deb`.** apt knows the package name, but no configured repository offers that version, because it was put there with `dpkg --install`. Detected on the source by asking apt where each manually-installed package's installed version came from and finding no repository at all. 308 309 **Unowned software under `/usr/local` or `/opt`.** An install script or an unpacked tarball dropped files there, bypassing apt entirely. Detected by listing the top-level entries of those directories plus the immediate contents of `/usr/local/bin` and `/usr/local/lib`, and asking dpkg which of them no package owns. The scan is deliberately shallow: it exists to *name* a finding so you can decide about it, not to walk and replicate a tree. 310 311 **A sideloaded snap**, and **a flatpak installed from a local bundle or from a remote that no longer exists.** Neither is handled today. Sideloaded snaps are detected, excluded, and replicated by nobody; the flatpak case has not been confirmed to exist. Both are deferred work — see the open questions. 312 313 Detection runs on the **source** only, because these are facts about what the source machine has. There is consequently no manifest of what was installed this way on the target, and so **nothing here is ever removed**. Removing hand-installed software on the target is manual work. 314 315 Every detected item ends the run in one of exactly three states: it has a snippet, it is marked machine-specific, or you skipped it for this run. Skipping for now is a real resolution, not an unresolved state — the tool does not nag you into writing a recipe. An empty snippet is not accepted as a resolution; you are asked again. Ctrl-C aborts the sync. 316 317 A snippet is **opaque**. It is stored and replayed exactly as written, and never parsed, interpreted, versioned or reasoned about. It runs as the target user with no privilege added around it — anything it needs must be written inside it — and it runs with no standing input, so a command that expects an answer fails rather than hanging the sync. The prompt where you write one says so, with a worked shape, because discovering that as a stuck sync is expensive. 318 319 Whether something is reproducible is judged by what the **source** holds. A snippet that exists only on the target leaves the item unresolved, because the source is the machine being replicated. 320 321 The snippet registry **travels**, unlike the machine-specific marks. That transfer is a whole-file overwrite, and it is gated: if the target holds an entry that the overwrite would lose or change, you are shown exactly which entries and asked. Declining aborts the run, and so does a run that cannot ask — the alternative is silently discarding snippets only the target has, and aborting lets you consolidate the two registries by hand. 322 323 A snippet you write during a review is persisted, transferred and replayed in that same run. You do not write a recipe and then wait a sync for it to take effect. 324 325 A snippet that has vanished between planning and replay, or whose replay fails, fails as its own item naming it, and the run continues. 326 327 ## When something goes wrong 328 329 Failures are attributed to the smallest thing that can carry them, and the run gets as far as it can. 330 331 Every approved item is attempted. A failure is collected with its own error, and all of them are reported together at the end, each naming its item. One failed item does not block the rest of its ecosystem, and one failed ecosystem does not stop the others. 332 333 A write that has no item of its own — a repository file, a signing key, a flatpak remote — fails against every approved package or application that needed it, naming what failed and why. You decided about software, so that is where the failure lands. 334 335 A read that does not answer is different in kind and is treated differently. If a package manager cannot be queried at all — a lock is held, a daemon is down, a status file is unreadable — the tool refuses to read that silence as "this machine has nothing installed", which would propose removing everything on the other machine. It fails once, naming the command that failed. An *empty* answer is not the same thing: a machine with no snaps is an ordinary machine and is handled as data. 336 337 **Today a failed read ends the whole run**, not just the ecosystem it belongs to. Whether that is right is an open question below. 338 339 An ecosystem reports success when it did what your review approved, including when the review was empty because the machines already match. It reports skipped when it deliberately did nothing — a run with nobody to answer, or the Ubuntu Pro gate — in which case it says why, records nothing, transfers nothing, leaves the target untouched, and does not affect the run's exit code. 340 341 ## What this deliberately does not do 342 343 Each of these is a real cost, accepted knowingly. 344 345 **The target's apt configuration is not under your line-by-line control.** Repositories, keys and pins appear because you approved a package, and declining the package is the only way to decline them. The two machines' apt configurations are converged for what packages need, not made identical. 346 347 **A pin cannot be kept on one machine only.** It returns on every sync until it is deleted on the source. 348 349 **A package you installed by hand on the source, but which arrived on the target as an automatic dependency, is not protected from collateral removal.** If the target's apt installed it, the target's apt owns it, and reclaiming it as your choice on the strength of the other machine's bookkeeping would be a guess. 350 351 **Machine-specific marks are not consulted when protecting against collateral.** Software you marked "never offer again" can still be removed as collateral of an approved install. 352 353 **Enabling apt sync without the unreproducible-software job leaves hand-installed `.deb` packages replicated by nobody.** They are silently absent from the review rather than offered as installs that would fail. 354 355 **Version drift is reported and never resolved**, for apt and flatpak. Aligning two machines' versions is your job. 356 357 **Cross-vendor divergence is reported and never resolved.** Where both machines have the same software from different vendors, the tool will not pick one. 358 359 **Hand-installed software is never removed from the target.** No record is kept of what was put there. 360 361 **Sideloaded snaps are replicated by nobody today.** Not because they cannot be — they can, with a snippet — but because the handoff is not built. 362 363 **A target with no Ubuntu Pro attachment costs the whole apt job for that run**, not only the ESM repositories. 364 365 **A review cannot be answered without a terminal.** There is no file of standing answers and no assume-yes option. 366 367 **Machine-specific marks are per ecosystem, per machine, and never synced.** A new machine means deciding again. 368 369 ## Open questions 370 371 Genuinely undecided. An answer invented here would be worse than the question. 372 373 Should a failed package-manager read fail only its own ecosystem, or stop the whole sync? Today it stops the sync, which is inconsistent with the rule that one ecosystem's failure does not stop the others. The argument for stopping is that a dead package manager means the machine or the tool is broken, which is not a finding about any item and may well invalidate the rest of the run. The argument against is that a broken `snap` says nothing about whether apt can be synced. 374 375 Should the ordering rule — software before folder sync — cover snippet-installed software as well? It covers the three package managers today. Snippet-installed software writes its own stock defaults exactly as an apt package does, which is the entire reason for the rule; the shipped configuration has it in the right place, but nothing catches a hand-edited configuration that moves it. 376 377 Should apt's and flatpak's repository-conflict questions cover the same set? apt asks about every differing repository file that feeds machine-specific software, and approving forces the write. flatpak asks only about remotes something approved this run would touch anyway, so answering "overwrite" cannot by itself make a remote travel. The asymmetry follows from flatpak having no always-sync bucket, but it has never been ruled on. 378 379 How many answers should apt's own behavioural configuration offer? It currently carries the full three-way decision including the permanent mark, reasoned from the fact that the restricted screens were justified by consequences a configuration file does not have. That reasoning is sound but was never ruled on. 380 381 Should deleting a repository ever be markable machine-specific? Today it is not, with consolidating the two machines' configurations as the stated remedy. That remedy is real work you may not want to do, and the alternative was rejected rather than tested against use. 382 383 How much does the Ubuntu Pro hazard actually cost on a real desktop? Measured in a container, zero of thirteen upgradable packages had an ESM candidate. That a desktop with a large `universe` set has many more follows from how apt ranks candidates, but has not been measured. The gate does not depend on the count; the size of the problem is unknown. 384 385 How often is a package manually installed on the source and automatic on the target — the case the collateral protection gives up? Nobody has counted. "Rare" is not a claim this document makes. 386

Two things you cannot mark, and the reason is the same for both. Deleting a repository, deleting a pin, resolving a repository conflict, and deleting or repointing a flatpak remote all take two answers — do it, or leave it for now — and record nothing. A permanent machine-local mark on configuration whose whole purpose is to feed software would silently and permanently change where that software comes from. Where two machines' configurations genuinely differ on purpose, the remedy is to consolidate them, not to record a preference that quietly diverges them further. Report-only findings — a version difference, a cross-vendor divergence, a package whose origin cannot be replicated — cannot be marked either. No machine holds a version difference. A permanent mark there would stop the package syncing altogether rather than stop reporting the drift, which is not what you would be asking for. These are resolved by fixing the underlying condition. ## apt apt carries every hard problem, so it gets the most space. The other ecosystems are largely apt with pieces removed. Scope is the **manually installed** package set — what you asked for, not what apt pulled in to satisfy it. Dependencies are the target apt's business to resolve for itself. Along with the packages come the repositories and pins that govern where they come from, apt's own behavioural configuration, and apt holds. ### Installing A package the source has and the target lacks is offered for install. What it takes to make that install faithful depends on where the source got it. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["On the source,
absent on the target"] --> B{"Where did the
source get it?"} B -->|"the distribution"| C["Ordinary install"] B -->|"a vendor"| D{"Does the target already
offer it from that vendor?"} D -->|yes| C D -->|no| E{"Can the source's origin
be replicated?"} E -->|yes| F["Install, naming the vendor.
Its repository, key and pin
travel as a consequence"] E -->|no| G["Report it, with origin
and reason. Do not install"] F --> H{"After the configuration lands,
what would apt really install?"} H -->|"the source's vendor"| I["Install"] H -->|otherwise| J["Refuse this one install,
naming both origins.
Continue the run"] ``` Two things about that diagram carry most of the weight. When an install would come from anything other than the distribution, the review says which vendor — you should not approve `gh` without knowing it is arriving from GitHub rather than from Ubuntu. And the last step is a real check, not a formality. Everything before it is preparation; only that step looks at what the target's apt would *actually* do after this run's configuration has landed and its package lists have been refreshed. A repository can fail to write, a pin can fail to win, and Ubuntu's own epoch can outrank every version a vendor publishes. So the guarantee is verified against the target's real state rather than inferred from the plan, and an install that would come from the wrong place fails as its own item naming both origins, while everything else in the run proceeds. Two machines pointed at different Ubuntu mirrors are not two vendors. Each machine's own distribution source files define what "the distribution" means for that machine, so mirror differences never read as provenance differences. Software installed from a hand-downloaded `.deb` is not apt's business at all — apt on the target has never heard the name, so an apt item for it could only fail. It belongs to the unreproducible-software section below. ### Removing, and reporting without acting A package on the target that the source does not have is offered for removal, in its own unticked group. Approving it removes the package without purging its configuration. A package present on both machines at the same version from the same vendor produces nothing at all — no line, no question. Three situations are reported and never acted on. Same package, same vendor, different version: both versions are named and nothing is done. Versions float — you install by name and take whatever the target's repositories offer. Deliberate pinning still replicates, through the pin files, which is the honest way to hold a version. Same package, two different vendors: reported as a provenance divergence naming both origins, and it takes precedence over any version difference on that package, because two vendors' builds share no version scale. Converging it would mean a cross-vendor reinstall you never asked for, and neither machine is wrong — only you can say which one is the odd one out. A package whose origin cannot be replicated at all — no repository file on the source declares it, or the one that does names a key the source does not have — is reported with the origin and the reason, and never installed from somewhere else. A package held on the target is never proposed for install or upgrade and produces no package-level line. Its hold is still an item of its own. ### Holds An apt hold replicates as its own item, decided separately from the package it applies to, in both directions. You may want a package synced and its hold not, or the reverse. An approved hold is applied after the package it names exists. Replicating a hold never changes the package's version, and a hold whose package failed to install fails alone. ### Collateral damage Approving an install can make apt remove something else. Whether you are asked depends on what that something else is. If it was installed automatically — apt pulled it in to satisfy some other package — the removal proceeds silently. That is the target's apt resolving its own dependency graph, and it is not a decision you have information to make. If it was **manually installed on the target**, you chose to have it, and you are asked before anything happens. The question names the package, says why it is protected — that machine's own apt has it marked manually installed, which is not the same as anyone having marked it machine-specific — and says what the approved change would do to it. Three answers, each stating its own effect: install anyway and accept the loss, skip and leave the triggering install unapproved, or stop. The stop answer says how far it reaches, because it ends the whole sync rather than this one ecosystem. The question is asked during the review, from apt's own simulation of the transaction, not as an interruption while packages are being installed. Declining cancels only the changes whose own transaction causes the collateral. This matters more than it sounds: the other answers in that review are yours, given about other software, and a decline that reached them would be a decision you did not make. So when a batch turns up manual collateral, each candidate is rehearsed on its own to find out which ones are actually responsible. Where the collateral is caused by a combination and by no single change, the whole set is cancelled and the question says so. Cancelling a change this way never alters a decision you gave for it. A package you marked "never offer again" keeps that mark even though the collateral cancelled it for this run. There is one case where you are told afterwards rather than asked beforehand: an install whose repository this very run must provision. Until that repository lands, the target's apt cannot resolve the name, and asking apt to rehearse a batch containing an unknown name makes it refuse the entire batch — which would strip the protection from every other package in the run rather than weaken it for one. Those packages are rehearsed individually after the repository configuration has converged, and unapproved manual collateral fails that one install. ### Repositories, keys and pins You are never asked to add or change a repository. A repository is written to the target because a package you approved comes from it, and a repository on the source that feeds no package this run syncs does not travel at all. Deleting one is different, because nothing derives a deletion. A repository the target has and the source does not is offered for removal with two answers. The request names the repository URLs the file declares, not just its filename — a filename is whatever created the file chose to call it, and the URL is what the deletion actually takes away — and it names the machine-specific packages on that machine that the deletion would strand. That second disclosure exists precisely because those packages are invisible in the review by design; without it you would see a bare file deletion and nothing else. It is disclosure, not refusal: deleting a repository whose packages are going too is ordinary cleanup. A repository present on both machines with different content is normally overwritten with the source's version, silently — you asked for the two machines to match. There is one exception. If that file feeds a package the target marked machine-specific, overwriting it would move the origin of software you explicitly told this tool to leave alone, and nothing else in the run would mention it. So you are asked first, shown **both versions of the file in full** — target's first, source's second, never a computed diff, because a diff of two repository definitions is not readable — and given two answers. Nothing is recorded either way. Declining is not a no-op: every approved package whose origin depended on that file fails by name, rather than being installed from somewhere else. The distribution's own source files are written when the target lacks them, overwritten when they differ, and never removed or offered for removal. They are what defines "the distribution's own origin" on each machine, which is what stops two machines on different mirrors disagreeing about every package. Files apt itself does not read — the `.save` and `.orig` copies Ubuntu's tooling leaves behind — are not treated as repository configuration in any direction. **Signing keys are never a review item, in any direction.** You think in repositories and packages; a key is only how a repository is made to work. A key the target lacks is copied byte-for-byte from the source before the repository naming it is written, whatever owns it on the source — vendors ship `.deb` packages carrying both a repository entry and its key, so refusing to copy a package-owned key would make such a repository permanently untrustable. A key the target has with different bytes is refreshed, which is what makes a vendor's key rotation follow you even though rotation changes no repository file; the exception is a key the target's own distribution packaging owns, which is left alone. A key that already matches is untouched. Keys are never fetched from a vendor. When you approve deleting a repository, a key that nothing on the target references any more may be deleted with it. That count is taken against the target's real files after the run's writes, so a repository you left unticked, one marked machine-specific, and one this tool never syncs all keep their keys alive. Only the directory that exists purely for this purpose is ever cleaned up; ambient and distribution-owned trust is left to accumulate rather than deleted on a guess. Pins are the one exception to derivation. **Every** pin file the source has is written to the target, always, without review. A pin decides which origin wins, which is exactly what origin replication turns on, and a pin naming an origin the target does not have does nothing at all — so replicating them all costs nothing and cannot get a per-package derivation wrong. The price is that a pin you wanted on one machine only comes back every run; deleting it on the source is the only cure. Deleting a pin the target has and the source does not *is* reviewed, because removing it can flip which vendor supplies a package at that machine's next upgrade. The screen prints each offered pin file whole, one block per file, for the same reason the repository deletion names URLs: a name like `99-vendor.pref` tells you neither which origin it favours nor at what priority, and those are the whole content of the decision. A pin is never read as a statement about the packages it names. A machine-wide pin would otherwise report every package on the machine, and would make a target-only package impossible to remove and impossible to silence. apt's own behavioural configuration — proxy settings, recommends policy, the things that govern how apt behaves rather than where packages come from — is reviewed in all three directions with the full decision including the permanent mark. No approved package implies whether such a setting should travel, and it is exactly the kind of standing preference you genuinely hold per machine. ### Ubuntu Pro If the source carries ESM repositories and the target reports no Ubuntu Pro attachment, you are asked before anything is written and before any other apt question, with two answers: attach the target now, or skip apt entirely for this run while everything else proceeds. The screen tells you what to run on the target to attach it. This is asked rather than handled because it cannot be handled: attaching needs a subscription token or an interactive browser flow, the source's own credentials are root-only and not reusable, and carrying a token would put a secret on a command line. It is asked rather than ignored because ignoring it fails in a way you would never trace back to a sync. The ESM repository indexes are public, so an unattached target's `apt-get update` succeeds and the ESM versions win candidate selection — and the failure surfaces much later, as a 401 when apt fetches the actual package for some unrelated install. Answering "I have attached it" re-probes the target rather than believing you, and you may answer as many times as you like. Skipping skips the whole apt job rather than only the ESM files, because pins always travel, so the source's ESM pins would otherwise land on a target without the sources they name — leaving a candidate selection that matches neither machine. An untouched configuration is a state you can reason about. A run with nobody to ask takes the skip and says why. A dry run does not ask; it warns that a real run would skip apt, because a rehearsal must not send you off to attach a machine. Only whether the target is attached is ever logged or shown. The attachment check also learns the subscriber's identity, and that never leaves it. ### Applying apt's changes All of the repository-configuration work a run does is applied as one unit: everything is backed up first, written in apt's own required order, and followed by a single refresh of the package lists. If that refresh fails, every file the unit touched is restored and `/etc/apt` is left exactly as it was found — a half-written configuration nobody reviewed is worse than either end state. Every approved package whose origin depended on that unit then fails, by name, and the run continues with the packages that did not. If a restore itself fails, the backup is kept and its path is named, because it holds the only remaining copy of that file. A derived write has no item of its own, so it cannot fail as one. Its failure is charged to every approved package that needed it, naming what failed — you decided about a package, not about a file. Every derived write is logged as it lands and appears in a dry run's preview: not asking is not the same as hiding. ## snap snap is the simple ecosystem with one sharp exception. There is one store, and a name resolves to one publisher through an assertion snapd validates itself. So there is no origin question, no repository, no key, and no screen for any of them. Nothing about snap provenance is ever put to you. The exception is that snap converges the source's **exact revision and tracking channel**, where apt and flatpak let versions float. The reason is that snap is the only ecosystem that puts the version number in the data path: per-user application data lives in `~/snap///`. If the two machines are on different revisions, folder sync has no correct thing to do — it would either skip the data or plant directories for revisions the target's snapd never installed. Converging the revision is what makes folder sync correct. A snap on the source only is offered for install at the source's revision and channel; one on the target only is offered for removal; a difference of revision or channel is offered as a single change naming both values; identical produces nothing. Removing a snap leaves snapd's own pre-removal snapshot in place. That snapshot is your only recovery path if the removal was a mistake. A snap whose revision the target cannot fetch fails as its own item and the run continues. Refresh holds replicate as their own items in both directions, decided separately from the snap. A hold recorded for a snap the source no longer has produces no item — the source is authoritative for what you currently intend. No command this tool issues ever sets a standing hold as a side effect. Sideloaded snaps — installed from a local `.snap` file rather than the store — cannot be reproduced by any snap command, because no store can serve their revision. Today they are named in a warning and dropped: no install is offered, and the target's matching entry is withheld too, so "cannot reproduce this" does not turn into "propose deleting it there". A sideloaded snap the source does *not* have is still an ordinary removal candidate. **This is a current gap rather than a settled outcome** — a snippet could reproduce one, and the intended fix is to hand them to the unreproducible-software path. Either failure fails that one application, naming both URLs. An application whose origin remote exists neither on the target nor among this run's own additions is refused as its own item naming the missing remote. A remote the source restricts with a filter is replicated **unfiltered**, and the run warns once per such remote and tells you how to re-apply the filter on the target. A mask is a pure pattern, so editing one reads as remove-old plus add-new and a scope split reads as add plus remove — reported as found, not normalised. Masks land after the applications, so a mask can never suppress a dependency an approved install needs to pull in. An installation that is neither the user nor the system one is skipped rather than guessed at.
